issues.legal_issue: A suit concerning a public religious trust falls outside the special public-trust procedure when its dominant purpose is to vindicate an individual’s right, or another person’s individual right, to hold an office.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought a declaration that a particular person was the duly installed head of the trust and asked the court to appoint him, or alternatively another person, to that office.
The plaint challenged the incumbent’s entitlement to the office but did not challenge the validity of the claimed appointee’s installation or allege mismanagement by him.
The plaintiffs did not implead or refer to other persons nominated to succeed the former head, despite relying on the custom of nomination.
The courts below found that the suit’s primary purpose was to establish the claimed appointee’s right to the office, and the Supreme Court found no reason to disturb that finding.
issues.conclusion: The suit’s dominant purpose was to vindicate an individual claim to the headship, not a public right of the trust’s beneficiaries, and it was therefore outside the scope of Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
issues.legal_principle: Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides a special procedure for suits concerning public religious or charitable trusts. The court must consider the suit’s dominant purpose, the capacity in which the plaintiffs sue, and the plaint’s allegations, rather than relying only on the reliefs claimed or the plaintiffs’ number or sanction. A suit primarily seeking to remedy an infringement of an individual right, including another person’s individual right to an office, does not fall within Section 92. The Court followed Sugra Bibi v. Hazi Kummu Mia, (1969) 3 SCR 83, and approved Shamukhan v. Govinda, AIR 1937 Madras 92, and Tirumalai Devasthanams v. Krishnayya, AIR 1943 Madras 466.

predicates.public_religious_trust_suit: The proceeding is brought by interested persons concerning the administration of a public religious or charitable trust.
predicates.individual_office_claim_is_dominant_purp: The suit’s dominant purpose is to establish or vindicate an individual’s claim, or another person’s individual claim, to hold an office.

issues.definition: When a suit concerning a public trust is chiefly brought to establish an individual’s claim to an office, it falls outside the special procedure for public-trust suits.

issues.legal_issue: A suit brought under the special public-trust procedure must fail when the alleged breach is not proved and the request for administrative directions has no factual foundation.
material_facts: The plaintiffs alleged that the incumbent had committed breaches of trust, but the trial court and the High Court found no evidence substantiating those allegations.

The plaint asserted that court directions were necessary for trust administration but gave no reasons or factual particulars showing maladministration or a defect in the administrative arrangements requiring correction.
The courts found the request for directions to be unsupported and made only to bring the suit within the special procedure.
issues.conclusion: The alleged breach was not substantiated and the request for directions lacked a factual basis, so the foundation for a suit under Section 92 failed and the suit was not maintainable under that section.
issues.legal_principle: Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure requires a suit to rest on an allegation of breach of a public trust or a demonstrated need for directions for its administration, and to seek one or more of the reliefs specified in that section. The plaint is considered in the first instance to assess whether the suit falls within the section; however, if evidence shows that the alleged breach was not made out and the request for directions is vague and without a factual or reasoned foundation, the suit must be dismissed. The Court referred to Association of B.D.B. Bagga Singh v. Gurnam Singh, AIR 1972 Rajasthan 263, Vahan Singh v. Achhar Singh, AIR 1968 Punjab and Haryana 463, and Radha Krishna v. Lachmi Narain, AIR 1948 Oudh 203. It did not decide the broader meaning of the statutory phrase concerning directions necessary for trust administration.

predicates.public_trust_procedure_suit: The proceeding is brought as a suit concerning the administration of a public trust under a special public-trust procedure.
predicates.alleged_trust_breach_is_not_proved: The evidence does not establish the breach of trust alleged by the plaintiffs.
predicates.administrative_direction_request_lacks_f: The plaintiffs request administrative directions without facts or reasons showing why the directions are needed.

issues.definition: A public-trust suit is not maintainable under the special procedure when its alleged breach is unproved and its request for administrative directions lacks factual support.
